subject: Computer Networking
title: RFID: Invisible Tags
description: A quick win: understand RFID: Invisible Tags.

hook.text: A warehouse scans 1,000 boxes per minute without opening them. RFID tags inside each box respond automatically.

buildup.text: RFID uses radio signals to identify tagged objects. Passive tags have no battery — the reader's signal powers them.

discovery.text: Tags can be read through cardboard, plastic, and fabric. No line of sight needed, unlike barcodes.

twist.text: RFID tags cost as little as 5 cents each. At that price, every product in a store can be individually tracked.

climax.text: Retail, logistics, healthcare, and livestock management all use RFID. Billions of tags are deployed worldwide.

punchline.text: RFID makes invisible inventory visible. No scanning required.

quiz.question: What advantage does RFID have over barcodes?
options: It can read tags without line of sight, through packaging

details.summary: Radio-Frequency Identification uses electromagnetic fields to read data from small tags attached to objects. Passive tags draw power from the reader's signal and cost cents each, while active tags have batteries for longer range.
details.whyItMatters: RFID automates identification and tracking of physical objects across supply chains, warehouses, and retail. It processes thousands of items per second without line-of-sight, replacing manual barcode scanning.
takeaways: Passive RFID tags require no battery and cost a few cents
Readers identify hundreds of tagged items per second wirelessly
No line-of-sight needed unlike barcode scanning

faq.question: How is RFID different from NFC?
faq.answer: NFC is actually a subset of RFID operating at the same 13.56 MHz frequency but limited to very short range and standardized for consumer interactions. RFID encompasses a wider range of frequencies and longer read distances.

faq.question: Why hasn't RFID replaced barcodes entirely?
faq.answer: RFID tags cost more than printed barcodes, which are essentially free. RFID signals can be affected by metal and liquids. Reading accuracy varies with tag orientation and environment. For low-value items where individual tracking isn't needed, barcodes remain more cost-effective.
